blocks.text: A **printer** is an **output device**. It turns digital text, pictures and graphics into a **hard copy**, usually on paper. Electronic information is called a **soft copy**; physical printed output is a **hard copy**.

blocks.title: Two broad groups
rows: Strikes an inked ribbon against the paper
Dot matrix, daisy wheel, drum, chain, band

blocks.title: Resolution is not speed
rows: **Dots Per Inch**: dots along one linear inch. Higher DPI generally allows finer detail, though paper, ink or toner also affect quality.

blocks.text: Printer converts **soft copy to hard copy**. Mechanical striking through an inked ribbon = **impact** printer. Resolution unit = **DPI**.

blocks.title: Printer connections
items: **Parallel port**: a legacy connection widely used by older printers.
**USB**: the common direct connection today.
Some models also use **Ethernet** or **Wi-Fi**.
A parallel port is one printer interface, not the only one.

blocks.title: Milestones
items: India's first printing press set up at St. Paul's College, Goa
Chester Carlson made the first successful xerographic image (electrophotography, later called xerography)
Remington Rand's UNIVAC high-speed printer, a landmark in computer printing
Gary Starkweather invented laser printing at Xerox
Andrew Gabor and the Diablo team developed the successful daisy wheel mechanism
Diablo HyType (daisy wheel) shipments began
Chuck Hull's first successful SLA 3D-printed part
HP ThinkJet: first mass-marketed personal inkjet printer

blocks.title: Do not mix these up
blocks.text: A **printing press**, a **photocopier** and a **computer printer** are different things. Carlson's invention was electrophotography (xerography), not every kind of printer.

items: A **serial impact printer**, usually classified as a **character printer** in basic exams.
**Pins or wires** strike an inked ribbon to make patterns of dots.
Common printheads have **9 pins** or **24 pins**.
Prints text and basic graphics; the mechanical action is **noisy**.
Speed is commonly stated in **CPS** (Characters Per Second).
Major strength: it can print **multipart forms, carbon copies and carbonless copies** in one pass.
Used for invoices, continuous stationery, records and **bank passbooks**.

blocks.title: Cost and history claims
blocks.text: Dot matrix is traditionally called economical, but the price depends on the model; a specialised dot matrix printer need not cost less than an entry-level laser. 'Dot matrix was the first impact printer' is **not** a reliable historical claim. Dot matrix printers are noisy, not silent.

A **daisy wheel** printer is an impact **character printer** whose print element is a wheel with petal-like spokes. Each spoke carries a **preformed** letter, number, punctuation mark or symbol. It is also nicknamed the **petal printer**.

blocks.title: How a daisy wheel prints
items: Wheel rotates
Spoke aligns
Selected character lines up
Hammer strikes
Presses spoke on the ribbon
Character appears
On the paper
Produces clear, **typewriter-style** (letter-quality) text; popular in the 1970s and early 1980s.
Limited to the characters on its wheel; changing the wheel changes the typeface.
Relatively **slow and noisy**; unsuitable for general graphics.
Andrew Gabor and the Diablo team developed the successful mechanism around 1970; HyType shipments began in 1972.

blocks.title: Golf ball is different
blocks.text: A **golf-ball** print element belongs to the **IBM Selectric** typewriter. It is not another name for a daisy wheel. Also, silent operation is **not** a daisy wheel feature.

sections.title: Character vs Line Printers: Drum, Chain & Band

rows: Produces a complete line during one printing cycle

blocks.title: Traditional line printers (all impact)
rows: A rotating drum carries raised character sets arranged for the print columns; hammers strike when the required characters reach their positions. Standard classification: **line printer**.

A moving chain carries repeated sets of raised characters; timed hammers press paper and ribbon against the required type. Usually **monochrome** (single-colour ribbon); suited to high-volume text and business records. IBM 1403 is a well-known chain-based line printer.
A flexible moving band carries raised characters. An impact **line printer**, like drum and chain.

blocks.title: Drum is not 'both'
blocks.text: Saying a drum printer is 'both a character and a line printer' is misleading in a basic classification question. The answer is **line printer**. Also remember: the chain carries **characters**.
Drum + Chain + Band = **impact line printers**; their speed is measured in **LPM**.

rows: **CPS** = Characters Per Second (sometimes CPM = Characters Per Minute)
**LPM** = Lines Per Minute (sometimes LPS = Lines Per Second)
mm/s, inches per second or labels per minute; page-based models may use PPM

blocks.text: **DPI** is resolution, never printing speed. The unit of speed depends on what the printer outputs: characters, lines, pages or length of paper.

blocks.title: Core features
items: A **non-impact** printer that uses a **laser beam**, electrostatic charges and powdered **toner** (not liquid ink).
Printing is based on **electrophotography**, also called **xerography**.
**Gary Starkweather** invented laser printing at Xerox in **1969**; Chester Carlson's 1938 xerographic work gave the underlying principle.

blocks.title: How a laser printer works
items: Drum is charged
Photosensitive drum gets an electric charge
Laser writes image
Selected areas change, invisible image forms
Toner sticks
Toner adheres to the image areas
Transfer to paper
Toner image moves onto the paper
Fuser fixes it
Heat and pressure bond toner to paper

blocks.text: The laser writes the image on the drum; it does not directly burn the document onto ordinary paper. Laser printers give sharp text and clear graphics and often suit frequent printing and large document volumes. Speed is commonly stated in **PPM** and resolution in **DPI**. Service life depends on the model, maintenance and workload.

blocks.title: Parts to remember
rows: Fixes toner using heat and pressure
Enables automatic printing on both sides of a sheet

items: A **non-impact** printer that ejects tiny **liquid ink droplets** through printhead **nozzles**.
Controlled droplets build text, photographs and colour graphics.
It does **not** strike an inked ribbon.
Speed is commonly in **PPM**; resolution in **DPI**.
**HP ThinkJet** (1984) was the first mass-marketed **personal** inkjet printer.

blocks.title: Careful with history
blocks.text: HP ThinkJet being the first mass-marketed personal inkjet printer does **not** mean HP invented every form of inkjet technology.

rows: A heated printhead activates a heat-sensitive coating on special paper
No ink, toner or ribbon: this is what 'inkless' most accurately means
Heat transfers colouring material from a ribbon onto the medium

blocks.title: Thermal paper and BPA
rows: Contains a dye, a developer and other components; heating causes a chemical reaction that makes visible marks, commonly black
**Bisphenol A**, formula C15H16O2, has been used as one developer; it is also used to make certain plastics and resins
Other formulations exist, so not all thermal paper contains BPA

blocks.title: Where thermal printing is used
items: Banking: ATM receipts and transaction slips.
Airlines and transport: boarding passes, tickets, baggage labels.
Grocery and retail: bills and customer receipts.
Entertainment: admission tickets.
Logistics: barcodes and shipping labels.
**POS** (Point of Sale) receipt printers commonly use thermal technology.
Traditional thermal-paper **fax** (facsimile) machines use thermal printing; plain-paper fax machines may use inkjet or laser.

blocks.title: Do not generalise
blocks.text: Calling every thermal paper 'bisphenol-coated' is an oversimplification. Direct thermal needs **heat-sensitive coated paper**, while thermal transfer needs a ribbon. Receipt speed is commonly in mm/s, not universally PPM.

A **plotter** is a specialised device for large, accurate drawings. It is used by engineers, architects, designers and mapping professionals for maps, blueprints, charts, building plans and **CAD** (Computer-Aided Design) drawings. It is the 'advanced printer' answer in exam options, because precision is central.

items: Traditional **pen plotters** trace continuous lines from vector paths and can be slow for complex drawings.
Many modern plotters are large-format **inkjet** printers that handle large sheets or rolls.
Professional models often cost more than basic desktop printers.
Computer plotters emerged in the late 1950s, worked with large systems including mainframes, and spread with CAD in the 1970s and 80s.

blocks.title: Plotter types
rows: A rotating drum moves the paper while the pen moves along the other axis
Paper stays still while the pen moves
Uses one or more pens, sometimes of different colours
Uses ink droplets for large-format output
Electrical charges form an image that attracts toner
A blade cuts programmed designs in vinyl or paper

blocks.text: Categories overlap: a **pen plotter** can be either a drum or a flatbed plotter.

**3D printing** creates a physical object by adding material layer by layer; this is called **additive manufacturing**. **Chuck Hull** is widely called the **father of 3D printing**. He developed **stereolithography (SLA)**, and his first successful SLA part dates to **1983**. SLA uses light to harden liquid photopolymer in successive layers.

blocks.title: Flat view vs object
blocks.text: A plotter or printer prints a **flat view** of a 3D design. A **3D printer** builds the actual object.

blocks.title: Duplex printing
rows: Printing on **one side** of a sheet
Printing on **both sides** of a sheet
The device that handles paper for second-side printing automatically
The user has to turn and reload the paper
Mechanical striking through an inked ribbon
Parallel port (USB and networking also exist)
Pins or wires making dots; multipart and carbon copies
Preformed letters on a wheel; slow, noisy, no general graphics
Chain carries characters; speed in LPM
Heat-based, heat-sensitive paper, receipts and tickets
Large, accurate drawings, CAD and blueprints

blocks.title: One-line memory aids
blocks.text: Daisy wheel = golf ball? **No**: golf ball is IBM Selectric. Drum = line printer. Thermal = heat. Inkjet = liquid droplets. Dot matrix = pins and dots.

revision: A printer is an output device that converts soft copy into hard copy.
Impact printers strike an inked ribbon (dot matrix, daisy wheel, drum, chain, band); non-impact: inkjet, laser, thermal.
DPI (Dots Per Inch) measures resolution; CPS, LPM and PPM measure speed.
Dot matrix: serial impact character printer with 9-pin or 24-pin heads; best for multipart and carbon copies; speed in CPS.
Daisy wheel: preformed characters on petal-like spokes; slow, noisy, no general graphics; golf ball belongs to IBM Selectric.
Drum, chain and band printers are impact line printers measured in LPM; a chain carries characters.
Laser: non-impact, laser beam plus toner on a photosensitive drum, fuser uses heat and pressure; Starkweather, Xerox, 1969.
Chester Carlson made the first xerographic image in 1938; Remington Rand UNIVAC printer in 1953.
Colour laser uses CMYK: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Key (black).
Inkjet ejects liquid ink droplets from nozzles; HP ThinkJet (1984) was the first mass-marketed personal inkjet.
Direct thermal uses heat-sensitive paper (no ink or ribbon); thermal transfer needs a ribbon; BPA is only one possible developer.
Thermal printing suits ATM receipts, tickets, POS bills and thermal-paper fax; receipt speed is usually in mm/s.
Plotters draw large, accurate CAD drawings, maps and blueprints; a pen plotter can be drum or flatbed.
3D printing is additive manufacturing; Chuck Hull (SLA, 1983) is the father of 3D printing.
Duplexer prints on both sides automatically; simplex is one side; India's first printing press: Goa, 1556.
